title: Coffee explains WTI with t = 69? Spurious regression, Durbin-Watson and the right critical values
concepts: residual ADF with ordinary vs Engle-Granger critical values

explain.prompt: An intern sends you: “log WTI on log coffee: coefficient 1.87, t = 69, R² = 0.69 — and the residuals pass an ADF at 6 %, so they're nearly cointegrated.” In 4–6 sentences with your table: why this is a spurious regression, what Durbin-Watson tells you (and does not prove), what the regression in differences shows, why the intern's residual test is wrong — and what is different about Brent.
rubric: Both series are I(1) with unrelated stochastic trends; regressing one level on the other produces a large R² (0.69) and a huge t (68.6) by construction: the usual t distribution does not apply when the residuals are non-stationary.

Durbin-Watson 0.016 is a strong warning sign (residuals almost a random walk; the Granger-Newbold rule of thumb: R² > DW), but not a proof — a cointegrated pair also has low DW in levels (Brent: 0.046).
In daily changes the relationship vanishes: coefficient 0.005, t = 0.25, R² 0.000, DW 1.97 — coffee does not move WTI.

The residuals of an estimated regression are made as stationary-looking as possible by OLS, so ordinary ADF p-values are too optimistic (0.059 here); Engle-Granger critical values give p = 0.17 — no cointegration.

Brent passes both tests (Engle-Granger p = 0.001; in changes, t = 66, R² 0.68) — but statistics alone would not justify it either: what makes Brent–WTI worth testing is the arbitrage between two crude benchmarks (transport, quality, export capacity). Without a mechanism, a cointegration test is a fishing trip.
